summaries.example: Imagine two maps of the same park. One map says the hill is made of one kind of material, while a newer map describes it differently. Yet both maps may keep the same paths and distances. A structural realist says that these lasting patterns may be the part of science we can trust most.
summaries.summary: Structural realism is a position in the debate about what science tells us about the world. Scientific realists say that our best theories are at least roughly true, including their claims about unseen things. Critics point to the history of science: older theories sometimes made successful predictions but were later rejected. Structural realism offers a middle path. It says that a theory can be wrong about the hidden objects or materials it describes while still getting important relationships, patterns, or mathematical rules right. For example, different theories of light changed their pictures of what light is, but some successful relationships were carried forward. Epistemic structural realism says that structure is the part of reality science can know, while the deeper nature of the things involved may remain unknown. Ontic structural realism goes further: it says structure and relations may be more basic than individual objects. These views face challenges. Critics ask whether structure can be separated from content, whether enough structure survives scientific change, and whether relations need objects to relate. The entry surveys these competing proposals rather than presenting one settled answer.
key_ideas: Science has often changed its ideas about hidden objects, such as what light or heat is made of.
Structural realism tries to keep some trust in science without claiming that every old scientific picture was correct.
It says that relationships, patterns, or mathematical structure may survive when the objects used to describe them change.
Some structural realists think structure is what we can know; others think structure is what is most real.
Philosophers disagree about whether relationships can exist without individual things related to one another.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us understand why science can make progress even though scientific theories change. It also asks a deep question: when scientists discover a successful pattern, are they learning about the world itself, or only organizing observations? Thinking about this can make us more careful about both trusting science and recognizing its limits.

important_terms.definition: The view that science may reliably tell us about the patterns and relationships in the world, even when its ideas about hidden things change.
The idea that successful scientific theories describe real things, including things we cannot directly see.
The view that we should be careful about believing claims concerning things that cannot be observed.
A pattern of connections, relationships, or mathematical rules.
A change in which an older scientific theory is replaced by a newer one.

questions_to_think_about: If a scientific explanation changes, what parts might still be useful?
Is a map useful because it names every object correctly, or because it shows relationships accurately?
Can there be a relationship without things that are related?
Should we trust a theory that makes accurate predictions even if its hidden objects are later rejected?

summaries.example: Consider the shift from Fresnel’s theory of an elastic light-carrying ether to Maxwell’s electromagnetic theory. The theories disagree about what underlies light: the ether was treated as a material medium, whereas Maxwell’s theory uses electromagnetic fields. Yet mathematical relationships connecting phenomena were retained or transformed into the newer framework. Structural realism interprets this continuity as evidence that science may preserve structure without preserving a theory’s full ontology.
summaries.summary: Structural realism addresses a tension within scientific realism. The no-miracles argument says that the predictive and explanatory success of science would be surprising if successful theories were not approximately true. The history of science, however, includes theories that were empirically successful yet later rejected, creating the pessimistic meta-induction. John Worrall’s proposal was that scientific change can preserve structure without preserving a theory’s full description of unobservable entities. Structural realism therefore aims to retain a realist explanation of scientific success while avoiding commitment to obsolete ontologies. Epistemic structural realism (ESR) treats this as a limit on knowledge: science can reveal relations, properties, or higher-order structure while leaving intrinsic natures unknown. Kantian versions connect this limit with the idea that things in themselves are not directly accessible. Other ESR proposals use Ramsey sentences, which replace theoretical terms with variables and describe what must exist to satisfy a theory’s formal role. Critics argue that this may preserve only observational content, because formal structure can be realized by many different relations; this is the Newman problem. Ontic structural realism (OSR) is more metaphysically ambitious. It gives structure or relations a fundamental status and has been developed in response to quantum physics, gauge symmetries, quantum field theory, and general relativity. Its forms range from eliminating individuals to claiming that objects lack intrinsic natures or receive their identity from relational contexts. key_ideas: Structural realism was proposed as a response to a conflict between the no-miracles argument for realism and historical arguments from radical theory change.
Its central claim is not that every mathematical feature survives theory change, but that well-confirmed relations among phenomena may be retained, sometimes as limiting cases or correspondences.
ESR is primarily epistemological: it restricts what we should believe or claim to know. OSR is metaphysical: it changes the proposed ontological priority of objects, properties, and relations.

Kantian versions treat the intrinsic natures of unobservable entities as inaccessible while allowing knowledge of their relations. Ramsey-sentence versions describe theoretical entities indirectly through their roles in a theory.
The Newman-style objection argues that purely formal structure may fit many possible relations and therefore may not uniquely identify the intended physical structure.

OSR is motivated partly by physics, including questions about quantum entanglement, particle individuality, symmetry, and spacetime, but its defenders disagree about whether objects are eliminated, relationally individuated, or merely dependent on structure.
summaries.why_it_matters: Structural realism connects scientific method, the history of theory change, logic, mathematics, and metaphysics. It offers a way to interpret scientific progress that is neither a simple claim that current theories are wholly true nor a conclusion that successful theories merely organize observations. Its debates also show how developments in physics can challenge familiar ideas about objects, identity, and what it means for a theory to describe reality.

important_terms.definition: A form of scientific realism that limits epistemic commitment to the structural or relational content of successful theories, while suspending judgment about intrinsic natures.
A metaphysical view that gives relations or structure ontological priority over, or independence from, individual objects and their intrinsic properties.
The argument that science’s success would be extraordinarily unlikely unless successful theories were at least approximately true.
An argument from past scientific failures: because successful older theories were later rejected, current theories may also eventually be abandoned.
The claim that different theories can fit all the same observable evidence, leaving the evidence alone insufficient to choose among them.
A formal reformulation that replaces theoretical terms with existentially quantified variables, preserving a theory’s stated structural organization while avoiding direct naming of unobservables.
A relation or property that remains unchanged under a relevant transformation; invariance is often used to identify objective structure in physics.
A pattern that supports simplified prediction and explanation within a particular domain, even if it is not fundamental at every scale.

questions_to_think_about: Does retaining empirical and mathematical structure provide a genuine explanation of scientific success, or does it collapse into ordinary realism or empiricism?
If two theories share observable consequences, what additional reasons could justify preferring one structural description?
Can relations be ontologically fundamental if relations ordinarily seem to require relata?
Does quantum entanglement support a relational ontology, or can standard objects and intrinsic properties be retained?
How should a structural realist explain the difference between mathematical structure and physically instantiated structure?

summaries.example: Suppose a school builds a model of a storm. An early model says the storm moves because of invisible spinning wheels in the air. A later model rejects those wheels but keeps useful rules about how pressure, wind, and movement are connected. A structural realist might say the early model had the wrong hidden story but captured some real structure that the later model improved.
summaries.summary: Structural realism is a family of views about what scientific theories tell us. Scientific realism says that successful theories are at least approximately true, including their claims about unobservable entities. Antirealist arguments emphasize that science has repeatedly replaced theories that once made successful predictions. Structural realism tries to respond to both sides. It holds that scientific change may preserve important structure—relations among phenomena, mathematical organization, or patterns used for prediction—even when the theories’ descriptions of hidden objects are abandoned. This is why it is sometimes called an attempt to get the “best of both worlds.” Epistemic structural realism, or ESR, is mainly about knowledge. It says we may know how unobservable things are related without knowing their intrinsic natures. Some versions connect this idea with Kantian arguments about limits on human knowledge. Others use Ramsey sentences, which replace theoretical terms with variables and describe entities through their roles in a theory. A major criticism is that formal structure may be too easy to realize: many different relations could have the same abstract pattern, so structure alone might not tell us what the theory is really about. Ontic structural realism, or OSR, makes a stronger claim about reality itself. It gives relations or structure priority over individual objects, especially in interpretations of quantum physics and spacetime physics. Some versions keep objects but make them relationally dependent; others question whether fundamental individuals exist. Critics argue that OSR may not explain causation, individuality, or the difference between mathematical and physical structure. The entry surveys these disagreements and related forms of realism,
key_ideas: Structural realism is meant to combine a realist attitude toward science with caution about the changing history of scientific theories.
The important continuity between old and new theories may be structural: equations, relations, successful predictions, or patterns can remain while the theory’s objects change.
ESR says structure is what we can know about the unobservable world; OSR says structure may also be ontologically basic.
A Ramsey sentence describes what theoretical entities must do in a theory without directly naming them, but critics say this may not identify a unique physical structure.
Some OSR proposals say objects depend on relations, while more radical versions say there are no fundamental individual objects.
The entry presents several objections, so structural realism is a family of views rather than one single doctrine.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it asks what scientific progress really is. If theories change, we need to decide whether science discovers the world, organizes observations, or preserves a deeper pattern through changing descriptions. Structural realism also shows why questions from physics can affect wider philosophical ideas about objects, relationships, knowledge, and reality.

important_terms.definition: The view that science can tell us something real about the world, including about things that cannot be directly observed.
The view that the lasting part of science may be relationships and patterns rather than a theory’s picture of hidden objects.
A reason for realism: the success of science seems unlikely to be mere luck if theories are not roughly right.
A challenge based on past science: many older theories worked well but were later rejected, so present theories may also be replaced.
The possibility that more than one theory can explain all the evidence we currently have.
A version of structural realism focused on what scientists can know about structure, while remaining unsure about the inner nature of unseen things.
A stronger version claiming that relations or structure are part of what is most fundamental in reality.
A sentence made by replacing a theory’s theoretical terms with variables that say that some things with the right roles exist.

questions_to_think_about: When an old theory is replaced, is keeping its successful predictions enough to show that its structure was real?
Why might a scientist prefer a theory that explains more than what can be observed?
Could two different sets of objects have the same pattern of relationships?
Would relations make sense if there were no objects at all?
Is structural realism more convincing in physics than in biology or the social sciences?
